blocks.text: Among the small, dainty dogs that the wealthy are accustomed to keep in their rooms and that ladies let lie in their laps, for which reason they are generally called lapdogs, belong the Bolognese, the Maltese, the Angora dog, the little lion dog and the silk poodle. One of these dogs is mentioned in the Talmud. It says (Ketuboth 61b): “If someone forbids his wife to be active in the [p. 87] household, he must divorce her, because idleness leads to all manner of vice.” The Talmud extends this Mishnah saying to the effect that divorce must take place even if the husband himself permits the wife to pass the time with chess (אישקקיש, Échecs; in Ibn Ezra, in the well-known poem on chess: שקאקי, Italian: Scacco*) and with lapdogs. Here the dogs are called: גורייתא קיסנייתא, which Rashi explains by כלבים דקים. Regarding גורייתא there is no doubt that the word means dogs, see above p. 82; the second word קיסנייתא, on the other hand, presents some difficulty. Bochart (Hiero. P. 1, l. 2, c. 55, col. 664) would compare it with Casina, the word with which Plautus titles one of his comedies, and of which he says in the prologue that the comedy bears a dog's name (cum latranti nomine). But apart from the fact that the word “Casina” is a comic invention of Plautus, others would even read Canissa for it, but are no more fortunate in this, since this formation of the word from Canis does not otherwise exist at all, and the word is in any case merely invented by Plautus.

It is simpler and more correct to read קיטנייתא for קיסנייתא; this is also what the Sulzbach edition of the Talmud, which is available to me, has, and Naphtali also read it so in his מתנת כהונה on Wajikra Rabba fol. 186, col. 4. His words are: גור כלב קטן כדאמרינן בפרק אעפ"י דמטלא בגורייתא קיטנייתא פירש"י ז"ל בכלבים קטנים. Münster (in his Aruch s.v. קסם) translates correctly according to the sense: Catuli, Catelli.

In any case it follows from this passage that in the Talmudic period people had already begun to lay aside the Oriental aversion to the dog and were already acquainted with the Occidental hospitality toward this quadruped.

In Rosch ha-Schana 4a the words והשגל יושבת אצלו (Nehem. 2, 6) are interpreted: King Artachshasta (Artaxerxes, identified, however, by the Talmud ibid. with Cyrus, and by Rashi on Neh. l. c. with Darius) had a bitch with him and had intercourse with her; on the coitus of a dog with a human woman see §. 511; he is even said to have taught the bitch to drink wine; but in this strange legend one should probably simply think of the lapdog [p. 88] which was a favourite of the king, but which brought upon him that obscene suspicion,

In B. Kama 80a it is said: One may raise cats, monkeys (or hedgehogs, see §. 112), polecats and כלבים כופרין so that they keep the house clean (according to Rashi: of mice). In explaining כלבים כופרין Rashi wavers between small, dwarfish dogs and large hunting dogs, which one may raise because of their harmlessness. The latter explanation, however, is incorrect already for the reason that large hunting dogs (see the following §.) do not serve for catching mice. A guiding source for determining that name, however, is given by the Mishnah (Kilajim 1, 6). Here it says: “The כלב הכופרי and the fox, although they resemble each other, may nevertheless not be crossed with one another.” Maimuni and Simson explain it as the hunting dog kept by villagers (כפר, village); the latter adds: the כלב הכופרי is, like the fox, small.

If, however, as also appears, the qualifier כופרי is meant to indicate only the local reference of habitat, this assumption nevertheless seems to us untenable for a twofold reason. First, in that first Talmud passage the raising of the dogs is permitted generally for towns no less than for villages, which explains why Rashi leaves that qualifier entirely out of consideration. Second, Simson cites the Jerusalem Talmud, which counts the כלב הכופרי among the wild animals, which even R. Meir concedes, although the dog is counted among the domestic animals (see Kilajim 8, 6). R. Meir, therefore, who counts the dog among the domestic animals and the כלב הכופרי among the wild animals, cannot possibly have thought merely of the local factor in distinguishing the two kinds.

We therefore believe we are not mistaken in seeing in the כלב הכופרי the hybrid of the dog with the fox. Aristotle too (l. c. 8, 27, 8) reports that the Laconian dogs are hybrids of the fox and the dog; these dogs are called fox spitzes among us (see Voigt, l. c. 1, p. 301). Now since foxes, owing to the proximity of the forests, do indeed come closer to villages than to towns, those hybrids too may be met with sooner in the countryside than in more populous towns, which explains the name of the dog [p. 89]. The fox spitz is small, even smaller than the English spitz. In the Mishnah (Kilajim 1, 6) the הכופרי therefore stands in the same relation to the dog and the fox as the כרד mentioned there to the horse and the ass: the one as well as the other are hybrids (see article Mule); that the fox spitz can be trained to catch mice, or is perhaps already disposed to it by nature, will not be surprising*).

The hunting dog, Canis sagax, is not expressly mentioned in the Talmud, but it is by Rashi (B. Kama 80a). R. erroneously explains כלבים הכופרין as hunting dogs which were supposed to serve to clear the dwelling of mice; but apart from the fact that its breeding is rare, on which weight is laid precisely in the said passage, it also serves only for tracking hares and foxes, and occasionally also for big-game hunting (see Voigt l. c. 1, p. 295). Cf. the preceding article; cf. also §. 122, note*, where hunting with dogs is called קינוניא.
